title: A Circle of Radius 4: How Big Can the Triangle Get? | AMC 10-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: Line 1: the compact figure (y=7, z=8) draws itself, circle inside, '4' radius. Line 2: a red '÷ 2' slip card shakes (no numbers). Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: A circle of radius four sits snugly inside a triangle. How big can that triangle be?
One tiny slip here gives you exactly half the right answer.
Hi, I'm Vantee. Let's go triangle hunting!

scenes.visual: Question text left, compact figure right (A, B, C, circle, radius 4, the two 6s from A). Line 4: choices 42, 60, 81, 150, 162.
lines: A triangle has whole-number sides. Its inscribed circle has radius four.
The circle touches A B and A C at the points six from A.
What's the largest possible perimeter?
Your choices: forty-two, sixty, eighty-one, one hundred fifty, and one hundred sixty-two.

scenes.visual: Line 1: circle and its three touch points pulse, radius '4'. Line 2: the two '6' pieces at A glow; goal pill 'BIGGEST perimeter, whole-number sides'.
lines: So: radius four, six from A to each touch point, and we want the BIGGEST perimeter.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; question figure visible.
lines: Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Line 1: side demo: a point outside a circle, two tangent segments with equal tick marks. Line 2: pieces at A labelled 6 and 6; pieces at B labelled y, y. Line 3: pieces at C labelled z, z. Line 4: rows AB = 6 + y, AC = 6 + z, BC = y + z. Line 5: note 'AB whole ⇒ y whole'. Line 6: s = 6 + y + z.
lines: Welcome back! Circle fact: two tangent pieces from one point are always equal.
So both pieces at A are six. At corner B, call the two equal pieces y. At C, call them z.
Each side is two pieces: A B is six plus y, A C is six plus z, and B C is y plus z.
A B is whole, so y is whole. A C is whole, so z is whole.
Half the perimeter is one piece from each corner: six plus y plus z. Call it s.

scenes.visual: Line 1-2: centre I joined to A, B, C; three small triangles tinted, each radius 4 drawn to its touch point with a right-angle mark. Line 3: rows. Line 4: Heron. Line 5: s − BC = 6, s − AC = y, s − AB = z. Line 6: Area = √(s·6·y·z). Lines 7-9: equation rows.
lines: Now find the area two ways. Way one: join the center to each corner.
Three small triangles! Each has a side as its base, and the radius, four, as its height.
Adding them gives one over two times four times the perimeter. That's four times s.
Way two: Heron's formula. The area is the square root of s times s minus each side.
The magic: s minus a side leaves one tangent piece. That's six, y and z!
So Heron gives the square root of six times s times y times z.
Set the two areas equal, square, and divide by s.
Sixteen times s equals six y z. Halve it: eight times s equals three y z.
Put in six plus y plus z for s: forty-eight plus eight y plus eight z equals three y z.

scenes.visual: Rows for z alone, then a table y | z built row by row. Line 10: s and perimeter columns. Line 11: answer reveal 162, choice E.
lines: Let's get z alone. Move eight z to the left, then pull out the z.
So z equals eight y plus forty-eight, over three y minus eight.
The top is positive, so the bottom must be too: y is at least three.
Make a table! At y equals three, z is seventy-two over one, so seventy-two.
At four, z is eighty over four, which is twenty.
Five and six give eighty-eight over seven and ninety-six over ten. Not whole!
At seven, z is one hundred four over thirteen, which is eight.
At eight, z is seven: a flip. Now z is below y, so only flips are left.
So s equals eighty-one, thirty and twenty-one. Doubled: one hundred sixty-two, sixty and forty-two.
The biggest perimeter is one hundred sixty-two. That's choice E!

scenes.visual: Equation morphs: ×3 row, +64 row, factored row with expansion check. Factor-pair list with 'add 8, divide by 3' test per pair.
lines: Here's a slicker way: make a product. Multiply both sides by three.
The right side becomes one hundred forty-four. Now add sixty-four to both sides.
The left side factors! Three y minus eight, times three z minus eight, equals two hundred eight.
Each factor plus eight must divide by three. Let's test the factor pairs of two hundred eight.
Two and eight fail. One, four and thirteen pass, and so do their partners.
Same three triangles! One times two hundred eight gives y equals three, z equals seventy-two.
When would you pick this way? When you want every answer without wondering where to stop.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red with their story. Line 1: the 13-14-15 and 10-24-26 triangles drawn with the same circle. Line 2: 81 = s. Line 3: 2(3 + 72) = 150. Line 4: habit pill.
lines: Now the traps. Forty-two and sixty are real triangles with radius four, just not the biggest.
Eighty-one equals s, only HALF the perimeter. That's the tiny slip!
One hundred fifty is what you'd get if you left out the two sixes at corner A.

scenes.visual: New figure: circle radius 3, the two pieces at A labelled 4.
lines: Now the circle has radius three, and the touch points are four from A.
Whole-number sides again. What's the largest perimeter?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant figure visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Equation rows, short table, reveal 56 with chime at end of line 6, then the 7-24-25 triangle.
lines: Let's check. The area is three times s, and also the square root of s times four y z.
Square, divide by s: nine times s equals four y z. Put in four plus y plus z for s.
Get z alone: z equals nine y plus thirty-six, over four y minus nine.
Again y is at least three. Three gives sixty-three over three, so z is twenty-one!
Four and five don't work. Six gives ninety over fifteen, which is six. Then z drops below y.
So s is twenty-eight or sixteen, perimeter fifty-six or thirty-two. The largest is fifty-six!
It's the seven, twenty-four, twenty-five right triangle. Fantastic work!

scenes.visual: Key idea card with the figure: equal tangent pieces 6, y, z; Area = r × s = Heron.
lines: The big idea: tangent pieces from one corner are equal, so a few letters name every side.
Then find the area two ways: radius times half the perimeter, and Heron's formula.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
